title: Doubling and halving: an easier multiplication trick
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
Double one factor and halve the other to keep the same product. For example, 4 × 6 = 2 × 12 = 24. A factor is one of the numbers you multiply; the product is the answer.

Picture four bags with six counters each. Pour two bags into one larger bag, then do the same with the other two. You now have two bags of twelve. No counter has escaped.
sections.title: Same counters, fewer bags

sections.html:
Draw six groups of five dots. Circle each pair of groups together: you now have three groups of ten.

So 6 × 5 = 3 × 10 = 30. You changed the arrangement, not the number of dots. It is still the same idea of counting equal groups.
sections.title: Try six groups of five

sections.html:
Doubling only one factor doubles the answer. To keep the total, change both: half as many bags, twice as many counters in each.

For these examples, start with an even number of bags so every bag has a partner. The regrouping follows the multiplication properties explained by OpenStax.
sections.title: Why both numbers must change

sections.html:
Sixteen bags with five counters each become eight bags with ten each. 16 × 5 = 8 × 10 = 80.

Counting tens is handy here. Use the trick when the new calculation feels easier; you do not need it for every multiplication.
sections.title: Turn 16 × 5 into 8 × 10

description: Why does 16 × 5 equal 8 × 10? Pair a few bags of counters to see how doubling and halving makes multiplication easier without changing the total.
